messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is an eighty-year-old widowed South Asian man who served for decades with the United States Coast Guard and who, in the final years of his active service, was at the helm of a rescue vessel when a navigational error during a fog-bound coastal operation caused the boat to strike a smaller craft. The collision was sudden and catastrophic. A junior crewman was pulled from the water with severe spinal injuries that left him partially paralysed, and though the official inquiry attributed the accident to conditions rather than negligence, Rajan never accepted that verdict. He remembered the particular quality of the light that morning — grey-green water, salt mist hanging low over the shoreline, the smell of diesel and kelp — and it was into that sensory world that his mind returned without warning for years afterward.

Rajan retired shortly after the incident and moved into a small house near the Massachusetts coast, where he had expected to spend his later years quietly. Instead, the environment that had defined his working life became a source of dread. Walking along the shoreline — something he had once done daily — now meant exposure to the same grey-green light, the same salt air, the same quality of open sky that surrounded the accident. When those natural cues registered, his body responded before his mind could intervene: his chest tightened, his attention narrowed, and the fragmented pieces of that morning began to surface unbidden. The memories did not arrive as a coherent narrative. They came in disconnected shards — the sound of impact, a flash of orange survival gear, a voice he could not place — that refused to assemble into a whole he could examine or put away. When he tried deliberately to reconstruct what had happened, the sequence dissolved; yet when a siren passed his window, or when a neighbour's scanner crackled with emergency traffic, the sensory world of the accident returned with full physical force, as though he were back on the water, the deck tilting beneath him. In those moments the reliving was total — not a recollection but a reinstatement, complete across every sense at once.

Because the memories arrived so violently and so incompletely, Rajan came to believe that the only way to survive them was to prevent their arrival. He told himself, with increasing conviction, that the accident had not been as serious as he remembered, or perhaps had not happened quite as he thought — a form of magical thinking that offered brief relief but left the underlying material untouched. He forced himself toward positive thoughts, rehearsing gratitude and forward-looking images, and when fragments surfaced anyway he pushed them down deliberately. These strategies quieted the surface without resolving anything beneath it, and over months he noticed that the memories seemed, if anything, more intrusive — as though suppression had kept them pressurised. The effort of managing his own mind also fed a darker conclusion: that a man who needed such constant mental labour to stay functional must have something fundamentally wrong with him. He had come to believe, with the quiet certainty of someone who has argued himself into a corner over years, that the accident had happened because of the kind of person he was — careless, arrogant, constitutionally unfit for the responsibility he had been given.

That appraisal of his own character sat at the centre of everything. Because he was certain he was defective, he was equally certain that danger was never far away — that his judgment could not be trusted, that unfamiliar environments held risks he would fail to assess correctly. He stopped travelling anywhere he had not been before. At the veterans' community centre where he occasionally attended lunch, he chose his seat with deliberate care, positioning himself with his back to the wall and a clear line to the exit. He had also, paradoxically, begun taking small physical risks — driving too fast on empty roads, neglecting prescribed medications — as though some part of him had decided that a man like him deserved whatever harm came his way. Talking about the future with his daughter, who visited on weekends, triggered the same cascade: any forward projection reminded him that the crewman he had injured was living a constrained life because of him, which brought the guilt flooding back and, with it, the fragments. His daughter noticed that he deflected every conversation about plans or hopes, and it was she who finally persuaded him to seek help. What Rajan most fears, sitting in the intake room, is that a clinician will confirm what he already believes about himself. What he most hopes, though he would not say so directly, is that someone will tell him he is wrong.
